blocks.x: Okay, we'll do a little talking now. Let me see, I better put the place where we're recording. This is recorded at the Howard Tilton Library, Tulane University, and it's an interview with Bill Bourgeois, and today is December the 10th of 19... Okay, 1959. So we're gonna get your name on here first. All right. What is it? You mean my correct name? Well, you can give it if you want to.
It doesn't matter. Wilfred. Wilfred is your correct name. I've been called Bill ever since I was born, I guess.

Bill Bourgeois. And Florence, what's your name? You're taking pictures here. Florence, Florence. And I'm Dick Allen. Okay, let's see. We were just playing that Bosdell for a record of... Let's see, what was that? Waffle Man's Call? Waffle Man's Call. That's pretty old, isn't it? Yeah, 24, I think. And you said... That's about the year I started playing. Yeah, is that right? And you were saying he was good with the plunging music, huh?
Very, very good. He was excellent. And Skaggs, you say?
Skagg Leone, yeah. And what about him? We were talking about him and Fass, huh?
He was a very, very fine musician. And I think Fazzola was one of his... He was Fazzola's idol.
Yeah, I see. Sort of took after him. Yeah. And while we were talking, you mentioned Hank Kamen, one of the teachers here. You used to know him.

Oh, I know Hank for quite a while. We worked together in New York. What was that about Hitler's birthday? Oh, we played a birthday party, Hitler's birthday party at the Liederkranz Hall, which is the German hall there. And our leader of the band was a Jew. And if they had known that they'd have thrown him right out of the place. Who was it? Lou Lockett. Of course that wasn't his right name. They thought he was a German or something, huh? Yeah, Lockett, you know, any other, anything else but a Jew.
Yeah. That's pretty funny.
And we were drinking up the German beer, and it was very excellent, believe me.
But no more of that for you, huh? Oh, I can't drink anymore.
Let's see, where were you born, anyway? I was born in Louisiana, in a small town about 60 miles from here, called Garyville. Is that up the river? Yeah, that's between here and Luton.
I gotcha. Let's see, there's some other people from out in that neighborhood, musicians.
Quite a few, I imagine. Oh, musicians, I don't know of any. Offhand, I don't.
I think rap was from around Lutheran or someplace like that, a convent?
Convent, yeah, well that's right in that neighborhood, but across the river on the other side.
Garyville is on which side? On this side, same as Wallach, the east side. Did you hear any bands out there when you were growing up?

No, I moved here when I was about six years old, my folks moved here. And I guess from the age of seven I wanted to play music. And being the youngest of ten, by the time it got to me they couldn't afford it. And my sister studied piano and voice for about fourteen years. And I told them I wanted to play piano at the time, and no, go outside and play, you bother me, you're too much trouble and all this and that. So finally when I got old enough, my mind was so set on it that I quit high school to go to work so I could buy a musical instrument. And I went to get a trumpet, and it cost too much money so I bought the clarinet. And I'm still playing it.
That's funny. That's an odd thing. What kind of clarinet did you start off on?
Well the Albert system, which I still play, is no use changing now, I'm kind of late.
Well, I like the tone. Sounds good.

Well I don't think I could do any more, any better with the BAME system. And when I started the Albert was still quite popular. Most of the boys who were playing a long time now just changed over, but they sacrificed a lot of tone for easy fingering.
What day were you born exactly? April 14th, 1907. So you're relatively young to be playing an Albert actually, most of the guys now who are in your generation are playing BAME.

It seems like as though I came up just during the shift, just before the shift to the BAME you see. And I was playing for about three years and I decided to learn how to read music so I went to an old Professor Giuffre here.
Oh I've heard of him. What was his name, Santo?

Santo Giuffre. He was a very, very fine musician, very good teacher. And Eddie Miller and I started together and Eddie was always broke. So I'd go take a lesson and Eddie would meet me at my house and I'd teach him what the professor taught me. So Eddie calls me Professor today.
That's funny. So he's about your age?
Eddie is about three years younger than I am, approximately.
Let me see now. We were talking about your family. You said your sister studied piano and voice. Anybody else in your family musical at all?

Well, no, not too much. My mother had quite a nice operatic voice, a soprano voice, but she never would do anything with it. And the others, a couple of my sisters played piano. One of them used to fake play anything she wanted by ear, you know. She wouldn't take the trouble to study music. But then I went to Giuffre for a couple of years and everything I did I did wrong naturally. Had to learn how to play all over again. And I taught him how to play a saxophone. Is that right? Because he was playing at the Orphan Theater then and they told him he'd have to play saxophone. He didn't know the first thing about it. So one day he went for my lesson and he said, can you teach me how to play saxophone? So I did the best I could.
That wasn't hard I imagine families make that switch.

No, no. He taught solfeggio you know. And he could recite solfeggio fast and you could execute on an instrument. The guy was fabulous. He played with a lot of the great big symphonies around the country. He was from Milan, Italy. And he told me that he wanted to study violin. But in an old country like that you don't study what you want, you study what they think you're better suited for. So they started him on clarinet. And incidentally he told me that he had gone to school or to music school for several years before they ever let him touch an instrument. Just learn the music you know. Fazolo would start that way too. Learn solfeggio before he ever played.
Well that's funny. A lot of you fellas seem to have studied under the Italians. But you're not an Italian at all. No, I'm French. Entirely French, huh?
Yeah, both sides of them. In fact, let me see, I'm the fifth or sixth generation in this country, in Louisiana.
Let's see, now I wanted to ask you about some of those French songs. Did you ever hear any French songs when you were young?
Oh yeah, my mother used to sing quite a few of them. I think I just about forgot most of them, you know, little ditties and French folk songs, you know.
I wondered if they picked any of them up in the jazz occasionally.
I think they have. I've heard some of them recorded already.
Well that A-Law-Bah, they have several recorded songs.
Well that was Negro.
That's strictly colored.

That was a colored song. Because, you see, there were more or less three different French dialects in Louisiana. The Negro dialect and what they call a Cajun, and then the true French. My mother and father were both educated in Louisiana but in French. And at home conversations were all held in French. My mother would speak French to us and we'd answer in English. So then it finally came to a point that she'd speak half a sentence in French and half of a sentence in English, you know.
Well did you go to public school here in the city entirely? Yeah, I went to public school, yeah.
Well that's quite a long time ago.
Which schools did you go to?

Well I went to, when we first moved to New Orleans, I started at Live Oak, which is now a high school I understand. It was a grammar school then. And then we naturally moved around town until we finally found a neighborhood they liked, you know. And then I went to McDonough 18 for just what, about a year, and then we moved again. So I went to Benjamin Franklin, which is now a colored school. And I graduated from there, from eighth grade, then went to Warren Easton.
What kind of music did they have in the schools in those days?

There wasn't too much of a, I mean music wasn't a big thing in schools in those days, you know. They had a music class and they used to lend the instruments to the pupils, to the students. And I went to borrow a trumpet and I was too late, I'd just given out the last one. So that's when I made up my mind that I definitely had to play music. You know, I could taste it. And one thing I can say that I've done the thing I like to do all my life. I mean I'd rather play music than anything else I guess.
That's wonderful you can do it.
Yeah, so far.
Have you worked at any other jobs that might do anything?
Well during the war I got into the shipyard until I got pneumonia twice and I had to give that up. I became a welder. And boy you talk about hard work.
Well that's not like playing music at all. Not at all.
I used to get home from work in the afternoon and just barely make it through the front door and collapse on the floor in the front room, you know.
Did they have any teachers in high school? Any music teachers that you remember?
I think Palletti was at Warren Easton. He was the head of the music there.
Is that the same guy who used to be out at Spanish Fort?
P-A-O-L-E-T-T-I I think.
We have a picture of his concert band.
Well he was a teacher when I went to Warren Easton.
Let me get that picture for you. What were you saying? That's the same fella huh? Uh huh. It's a picture of Palletti's municipal Hussar band. Hussar band. A German band isn't it?
It was supposed to be I guess.
I don't know.
The Hussars were German weren't they? I don't know.
He beats me. I forget. I'll have to look that up. We got a dictionary guarantee. Tell us.
I had a flute like that. The wooden Maya system.
That's right. The BAME came in on the flute. He replaced Maya.
Yeah. I had a Maya system flute which I got from Fazola. He got from I don't know where and he bought a BAME system silver flute and then I got one and I traded the flute into Whirlands.
So Palletti was there at the school and-

I didn't study under him. I bought the clarinet dick and went home one Saturday afternoon and sat in front of a big long mirror and looked at my fingers, you see. And about three days' time, well I discovered all different kinds of keys. You see, in about three days' time I could play almost any tune I wanted. And five, exactly five and a half months later I was playing professionally. Couldn't read a note. You know, keys in there didn't mean a thing, no matter what key you're playing in it. It was all the same to me. And about two or three years later I decided to go and learn how to play it, do it the right way.
Did you make up your own fingering pretty much or did you arrive at standard and fingering?

Well no, I did a lot of fake fingering, you know, which you have to do. Of course clarinet you have to finger more or less a certain way to get the tones. It's like a trumpet trumpet, you can cross fingers, cross vowels to get sounds, but clarinet you can't. You have to close all the holes to get the desired notes. Then Eddie Miller came along, he was a youngster, he was a little younger than I, and he started playing and he had a world of talent. So we started playing together and then Doc Rando, who also played with Bob Crossby, came along playing alto sax. And we had a sax team and Rando was the only one who could read. And we used to fake three way home and anything. Just played right off, just like we were reading parts.
What was the first job you ever played, even without pay?

Oh the first job I played with a fellow by the name of Stevens, Ernest Stevens, who was from way downtown on St. Claude Street. He was a barber. And on the side he made up little concert groups. And we used to go in the parks and play concerts. That's when I was, oh gee this was so long ago. And then we played some jazz band jobs, you know, no piano, upright bass, horn and drums and trombone and trumpet and clarinet. I played a couple of the dance jobs and then I played in the old Millenburg, a couple of those all day picnics. What did Ernest Stevens play? He played the bass. Also the drums, he played drums or bass.
As a drummer I think he's still alive. Jack Lane told me about it.
He must be very old.
I'm pretty sure he's the one Jack Lane, because all those Stevens guys were drummers.
Well I mean drums was his main fort, you know.
And I played with him quite old, I guess for quite a few months.

And I was trying to learn how to read at the time, that's even before I went to Jufri, you see. Trying to, and I couldn't do so well. And we played in parks like the Bunny Friends Playground and St. Rock Park and those places.
When would that be? What day of the week?
No, I really wouldn't remember. It wouldn't generally be on Sunday.
It could be any day. Not necessarily.
During the night, you know. Oh, nighttime. Night, maybe seven o'clock at night.
What kind of tunes would you play on a job like that?
Old marches. All marches.
And you'd fake your way through all that, huh?
Quite a bit.
Who was in the band, Stevens?
The only one I remember was Stevens. I was just a kid at the time. I believe I was what, seventeen?
Was it a big band?
Oh yeah, it must have been twenty to thirty pieces. Quite a big band, you know, so it covered me up. No matter what I played, nobody knew the difference.
A lot of clarinet players.
Yeah, about three or four, and I probably was the only one who couldn't read. And I'd just fake along whenever somebody else played, I followed.
I see.
Then I got in with a little band with Eddie Miller and the other fellas, three Millers in the band, none of them related.
Was this the piano player?

No, Benny Miller played banjo and guitar, and Lloyd Miller played drums. And you might have heard of Kero, Irving Kero, he played trumpet. He works for the public service now. And we played jobs all the way down to Burris and all over the country towns and all of that.
Was there a trombone playing in the band?
No, no, no, two saxes and trumpet. And drums and piano. Who played the piano? Joe Harris. Harris' finance, he and his brother in the finance business now.
No bass? No bass. No, we didn't need that.
Just two rhythm and, well three rhythm, guitar and piano and drums. Two saxes and trumpet. Did you tell me the drummer? Lloyd Miller. Lloyd Miller, yeah.
Those are new names to me pretty much.
No, those fellas quit playing years ago.
Then I went to work in the dance hall, the Jitney dance hall. Stayed there quite a long time. That's where I got a world of experience.
Would the tunes in the Jitney dance hall be the same as the ones you'd play down at Burris?
Yeah, more or less.

The old standards and all the old pop tunes and things like that. In those days we had drums and banjo and piano and trumpet and clarinet in the dance halls. And the piano would just start a pickup and we automatically knew just what he was going to play, what I call a tune. We knew by the key. He started a different key, we just joined in and started playing.
Would you play as long in a Jitney dance hall as you would at Burris? I mean, would the tune have as many choruses as well?

No, no, no. It was quite short. We'd play about three choruses in the dance hall, you know, and then stop. And there was a very funny thing that all the fellas around that time used to come in and sit in and practice. And one night I left, I took my instruments out and I handed it over to Napoli Moore's brother, Jimmy I believe he started. And by the time I went to the lake with the banjo player. And when we came back they were still playing for us so we put our instruments away and went home. And that happened quite a few times. That's where Fazola learned to play. Fazola used to come in and sit in and he said, I'll play for you if you buy me a sandwich. So I said, how long are you going to play? He said, well, an hour? I said, well, it's a sandwich. I said, play for two hours and I'll buy you a sandwich and a drink. And Fazola used to come in there for you at first and say, you want to sit in and play? And the rest of the fellas said, get that kid out of here, he can't play. I said, no, let him play. And he said, Mr. Bill, which finger should I start on? Which note do I start on? Which fingers do I use? So I used to stand next to him and hum, and he'd play just what I hum. Before long he had the musical education already, see, he just had to get familiar with the instrument.
How did that happen?
He had been taught solfeggio and music before he ever got to an instrument, see, so after he got the hang of the instrument it was quite easy then. He just learned to coordinate the tool, you see.
Well how does a guy like that learn how to fake? That's something that's always fascinating to me.

Well fake is nothing but practice. People that can't fake have never practiced faking. To learn a fake, you play a tune and you try to play the same tune in a different key and in another different key and keep trying different keys until you can play it in any key practically. And you learn your instrument, you learn the sound of your instrument, that just, subconsciously you just play the thing without even having to think of what you're doing.
Now when the trumpet's carrying the lead how are you going to make up those variations? How does that come?
That gets mostly by ear. You play a third away or a fifth away, the harmony, through the chord, you run through the chord, you know.
Do you think about those chords much yourself?
Well you do at first but now I don't even think of the chords, I just know them.
It just comes to you.

When I hear the tune I know the chord, I just feel the chord more or less. You could call it a feeling, you know. And you just weave in and out through the chord and all around the melody. You stay away from his note more or less or you'll pass over it going to another one. But you never linger on the same note as the melody unless you want to, you see.
Now back when you were starting you say you studied more or less by yourself for say three years or something like that? Oh yeah, quite a while, yeah. And then Jewfree, how long were you under him?
Jewfree, I must have gone to him about two years. Any other teachers?
No.

And I went through that clozé method, which was about an inch and a half thick, you know. Clozé? Clozé, clarinet method. It's a complete method. It's a great big thing. And after you go through that thing boy, you've done some playing. And the old man, Jewfree, was a stickler. He had a baton and he counted time while you played. And if you made one mistake, you start from the beginning, or he'd reach over and tap you on the fingers with his Italian accent, broken English, you know. He said, don't be such a jackass, you play right. He was a character, a fine old man, a real gentleman, you know. Incidentally he had a son who was a sensational clarinet player, who became a doctor, Dr. Philip Jewfree.
I guess he doesn't play music. No, no, he hasn't played music.

He's practicing in some country town I understand. He was an admitting surgeon at a charity for quite a while after his internship. But the guy could play clarinet, gee, I mean legitimate clarinet, you know. He was sensational. In fact when the old man was late some days, the kid would give him a lesson. He was a good guy.
That's how good he was. When did you take up other instruments?

Oh, you just gradually pick things up, like saxophone. I never did, I just picked one up and fiddled around with it and learned how to play it. And from observation too, you'd watch other people do things. The same way with flute. You'd just pick it up and start noodling around with it and first thing you know, you'd play it.
Did you take up sax before you were with Jewfree?
Yeah, I guess so, during that time. I had a call, playing on a professional job you have to double, you see, so I got a saxophone in the meantime and just started playing it and that was it.
When did you take up flute?

Oh, later. I guess quite some time later I just got interested in playing it and saw other people playing it, so I decided to try to play one. Fasola had this wood flute and so he loaned it to me. And then I later bought it from him and I learned on that.
Was that during the Depression or before? That was before. Before the Depression you started?
Yeah, I'm playing 36 years now, you see.
So you've been on the flute quite a few years.
Yeah, I played, I worked in Hot Springs and I played with the Concert Ensemble and played flute there.
You playing with the jazz band too?
Also, yeah. I doubled clarinet, alto, tenor, bass-axe and flute. And it was a very easy job at the Arlington Hotel. We worked a total of eleven hours a week.
I bet that was Joe Caprero's band.

Yeah, I was in a dance band with Joe Caprero but the Concert Ensemble was under Mr. Grosso. But the men that played with Joe had to double with him. You see, three nights a week you played in the lobby of the hotel and you played concert, and then the other three nights a week you played the dance in the ballroom.
What year was that about?
Do you remember approximately? I was in 19, I was in 19, I was in 19, I went to New York in 1936, or that's when I came back, that was around 1939 or 1940.
A pretty big band at Caprero?
Yeah, well he had three saxes and three brass, standard, you know, and bass and drums, and he played guitar himself and piano.
It's funny to me that that was really before we got in the war, and yet big bands were going
then.
Yeah, they're still going. It's funny now, we've got prosperity, and we don't have more than, at the most, ten bands
of that size working active in the country. That's right, it's all small band things now. Since the war, the trend has changed.
How could a band like that be supported during the Depression?

It did, I guess it made it either less profit or people were satisfied with less money, that's what it was. The prices weren't so high and the salaries weren't high, and people were more or less accustomed to a cheaper way of living, and the food and rents weren't as high, and it all balanced.
How much would you get, say, at that? Oh, $35 a week was about a standard salary then. Who was with Caprero then?

Shorty Reese and Santobi, we were the sax team. And Al Moore, a boy from here, played trombone. And the two trumpet players were from a way out, I forget their names, one boy I remember was from Philadelphia. And well we were just about the only local boy, New Orleans boys, about four of us in a town. This old man Grosso was a concertmaster for Metropolitan for about eight, ten years. He really was a fine musician.
Where was he from?
He was originally from, well he was in the Italian, and then I understand that later he bought a ranch in Arkansas somewhere and retired.
Back to your early days, did you listen to records in those times?

Oh quite a bit. I used to go to the movie and hear a tune in a movie when the talking pictures first came out, and I tried to remember it until I got home and tried to remember the key that I heard it in, and tried to play it in that same key. Just more or less of a memory test. And then I tried to play it in all different kind of keys. The same tune until I more or less mastered it you'd say, you know, and then a key.
You got pretty near perfect pitch.
Well it's a funny thing, I can call out any key or any note if I have my instrument in my hand. Without it I can't.
That's funny.

That's just from training I think. I've trained myself that way. But if I hold my either clarinet or saxon I can tell you any note you're hitting without playing it myself. But to put the horn down I can't.
Would you take the clarinet to the movies with you?
No, no, that's why I used to try to remember from the time I got to the movies to the time
I got home. What bands did you listen to on records?

Oh, just about all of them. All the local bands, you know. At that time the Rhythm Kings were quite popular when I first started, and Johnny Beisdorfer, and Sharky, a lot of the colored bands I used to listen to. In fact we used to have dance parties at my house, my older brothers had a club and I used to give a dance every so often and hire one of the different bands, Pinky, Pinky Vodakovich at the time, one of the colored bands, different bands you know.
What was the name of the band Pinky was with?

Well it was Pinky and his melody boys. And they really played Dixieland those days, but they didn't call it Dixieland, they just called it jazz. But it was the same type of thing that we play now. But it wasn't quite, it was only music New Orleans people knew, it was that type. That's all they heard. Everybody played the same thing.
Was Pinky with the Owls later or before?
No he had been, wait now, no later he was with the Owls, because I joined the Owls just before they broke up at the very end. Oh is that right? Eddie Miller and I played with the Owls.
Who was in the Owls when you joined?
Dan LeBlanc and Frank Netto. And Frank had changed to bass and Julian Lane played trombone and what's his name now? Trumpet player.
Padron.

Bill Padron. And Dan LeBlanc played third alto. He had moved from bass to third alto. And Ormond Hug played piano. And I'm trying to remember the drummer. I can officialize him but I can't remember his name.
Is that the guy that's in some kind of carnival business today where he does decorations? Was this the guy that came in after Earl Crum?
That was after Earl Crum, yeah.
That'll come to you.
Johnny Brent. Oh yeah. He's moved to California some years ago.
Yeah he played with Turkin Murphy for a while. Did he?
I didn't know that.
Yeah he's on some record with Turkin Murphy. I was surprised to see that.
He's a nice drummer. Johnny played good.
Very good drummer. Was he a New Orleanian originally?
No he's from Shreveport, around that section. Yeah he's from around, Jeff Riddick and he I believe was from the same hometown. I think Shreveport.
Let's see, did we get a guitar player with the Owls?

Yeah, Angelo Palmasana for a guitar. He never did join a union. He just faded out and quit playing gradually and then all the rest of us, I believe we were in the union at the time or just before we joined the union. We played at the old Spanish fort, the opening of the new pavilion, on percentage, commission basis. And the first week we worked we got sixty cents a piece. Good Lord.
Good Lord.

But I think we made more than that but we just didn't get it. One of those things you know. So we tried it for two weeks and it didn't pay so we just quit. And from then on the Owls broke up after that. The individuals went on different jobs.
Well who was really the lead of the Owls? I never did guess.

At that time Frank Netto when I played with him. Pinky had left them and Crum had left them and a lot of, most of the original band had left except Frank and Dan LeBlanc and Frank Netto were the two original, two of the members from the original band.
Who would take the clarinet solos?

Between Eddie Miller and myself. I was playing ten at the time and Eddie was playing lead alto and Dan was playing third alto. So Eddie played most of the clarinet, and most of the clarinet worked at the time.
What did Dan do on third alto? Would he play any solos much? Very seldom.
I mean he could play the parts but he wasn't a soloist because he had played bass so long he wasn't too familiar with the saxophone. He wasn't free on it in other words, you know, to take choruses.
It's funny, I like his bass playing tuba. He's a wonderful bass player.
Dan played very good.
Very good tuba on those old records.

He's an excellent musician. At one time we used to get together at Dan's house in afternoons, five saxophone players. And Dan used to scribble little things out and write things for the tunes like Deep River and all pretty things just for the saxophones to play, you know, in afternoons and drink beer and have more or less a saxophone session, a session of saxes, you know. Who would those guys be? Doc Randeau and Eddie Miller and myself and Almond Hug played piano and a couple other fellas, like probably fellas that quit playing by now like Frank Holomaze. D dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Okay, let's see. I think you'd better get a little closer to the mic. We were talking about Dan LeBlanc going over to his house.

Yeah, with his afternoon sessions, drink beer, and a whole crowd of saxophone players, just to see how it sounds. And well it went on like that. The fellas different jobs working around. And then in 1936 I went to New York, just on my own, and just decided to go and see what it was. And I worked around different clubs in New York, you know. And then Sharky came up there right after. I was working on a job in Brooklyn, and he begged me to come to work with him at Knicks. And incidentally we had this Henry Adler who is quite a famous teacher now, drums and drum teacher in New York. He played with us in Knicks. And George Ebrunas played trombone. And I made a movie short for Warner Brothers. It was the first time I think I ever recorded, was on this movie short.
Had you planned to make records with Sharky?
Well, some funny thing happened that Sharky made quite a few records, but he never did use me. And I was on the same job with him.
That's funny. I think he was using Joe Marcella.

Joe Marcella, yeah. Joe had the band at the Hickory House then. I think it was for business reasons, you know, trying to get himself up a little bit. And we even roomed together. Sharky and I lived together. But he used somebody else on clarinet, Joe Marcella, most of the time I think. And we played at Knicks and then we played at the Yacht Club on 52nd Street, at the Village Barn, quite a few places around there. And then my father died and so I decided to come home, try to make the funeral now. I missed it incidentally. And just around that time Irving Aronson had a staff band, which was at WGN I believe, and he offered me to come to work with him playing third alto and jazz clarinet. And Fazola at the same time quit Glenn Miller to go with Bob Crosby. So Fazola recommended me to go with Glenn Miller. So Eddie Miller was in town at the time and he recommended me to Glenn Miller and I was supposed to go to rehearsal. And I had to call him off, call him up and tell him I was off because I was coming home. And Irving Aronson told me if I came back within three months the job was still open for me. But I never did get back until last year I went there just for a couple of weeks for a vacation trip.
When did your father die?
That was 1939.
Now up in New York, who was Sharky using for you one day?

Nobody. I'm the first one he used. Because he got the job at Nix you see. He had some record dates and Fazola played with him on the record dates, the first dates. Because I went to the rehearsal, I mean to the recording sessions with him. And I even spoke on one record and didn't play. What did you say? Somebody said, Benny Pollack got the date for Sharky and he played drums. And the opening lines was, hey Sharky, what you doing up here in New York? And I answered, I said, man can't you see I'm trying to play the blues? Or a thing called Mud Hole Blues. Did you ever hear that record? I think I have it.
You probably have.

And I went with Fazola the first session he made with Bob Crosby. I went with him and he was nervous. He was shaking like a leaf. He said, come with me Bill. He says, man I'm scared. I said you're scared to play with those fellas. I said you should know those fellas better than anybody else. I mean, from your own hometown. He had played with Claude Thornhill and everybody else and he was scared to play with Bob Crossford's band. So they were stuck for something to play and I suggested that the March of the Bobcats, which wasn't called that. We used to sing it as John McDonough in the grammar schools. And Papa Celestan originated the trumpet chorus. You remember the chorus they used to that? Oh yeah, I know the trumpet chorus. I hummed it to Yank Lawson at the recording session and they cut it right there. And it more or less was my brainchild that they made so much money on. And it was a real spontaneous chorus Fazola took. He didn't practice anything else. He just played it and that was it.
And that was his first session with the Bob Crossford band.
Then he went to work with them steady, you see. His first job with them was the record date.
Oh yeah. Back to Sharky and Nick's, who else was in the band? Who was the piano player?

We had several, but the one who stayed along with us was a boy from Philadelphia, Del Zane, Z-A-N-E. It's new to me. Well he played on a radio station in Philadelphia for quite a while. What was the big station there? W-P-E-N is one. No, it is not the one, the other one. He was a staff pianist on that station for quite a while. Excellent piano player.
Did you have a bass player there?

W-P-E-N-E. We took Bradley and Johnny Castang came to New York. He played drums with us. When Henry Adler left, we used Johnny Castang. And of course he wasn't supposed to play because he just got to New York. He didn't have his union card, but we arranged it with the union and it was very nice to let Johnny come in on the job.
Did you have a guitar, a banjo?

W-P-E-N-E. No, no guitar. Three rhythm and three horns, six pieces. And we made that Saturday Night Swing Session, CBS had at the time. And I believe we broke the record by going back within a month. Nobody had ever repeated on the program. And Ted Husing was more or less our very godfather. He came in next and he liked the band so much that he arranged for us to go on that Saturday night swing session.
I'm wondering about that now. Sharpie had a guitar player named Bill Bourgeois or something.
No, no, it was me, Bill Bourgeois. But later we had Clayton Doerr, what he called Sunshine, played guitar. He had real thick glasses, close, near-sighted.
D-O-E-R?
D-O-E-R-R I believe it is.
Let me show you what I mean about Sharky having a guitar player. Hold on a second, I'll turn it off.
Meyer Weinberg. That must be New Orleans, huh? Yeah, Julian Lane, Meyer Weinberg, Dave Weinstein, tenor, Ormond Hubb. But I wasn't on there. Bill Bourgeois on bass, August Schilling on drums.
That sounds like a New Orleans band. I didn't know Ormond ever went to New York.

No, he didn't. Because Meyer Weinberg, Dave Weinstein either. He's the president of the union here. This is a misprint. These tunes we used to do in Nick's. Swing in, swing out, yes she do, no she don't. Yeah, we used to do those tunes in New York, see, at Nick's.
Here's the session you're talking about.

The next one. The band we used to call, Sharky called the band the Sharks of Rhythm while we were in New York, see? Santo and Irving Fazola, Clyde Hart, this is the record he made in New York. Frank Federico, yeah. Thurman Teague bass, and Benny Pollack, because Frank was playing with Benny Pollack and so was Thurman Teague. And this Clyde Hart is a colored boy.
Yeah, that's a good session. They have those in the public library. They have those.

This is the record I was telling you about, Mud Hole Blues, see? Moe Zutikoff, Trombone, yeah, and Joe Marsali, see? Joe Bushkin, who is quite famous today, Eddie Condon, Marty Shapiro, and George Wettling. Yeah.
Now that's when he was at Nick's he made those, but he switched the band around, right?
That's right, see, he used different fellas. Because all these tunes we were playing at Nick's, and he used the same tunes on the recording session.
What was he using Moe Zutikoff with, he had Brunis?
I can't understand that. I don't know. Well, he and Brunis were always at each other's throats. Never could get along together.
Eddie Condon, no.
Yeah. Now here's one with Brunis, you see, and Joe Marsali, and Joe Bushkin, Eddie Condon, and Fred Whelan, and Al Seidel on drums. But that wasn't... I was playing with him at the time, 1937.
That wasn't the next band hardly at all except for Brunis, huh?

No, no, yeah, that's right. Now his one was, this was recorded in New Orleans, you see, Santo and Lester Bouchon, Jeff Riddick, Tink Morton, Monk Hazel, 1940. No, that's 49. I remember. Yeah, I remember. I remember.
When those came.
Well this is the band that was playing at the famous door with him.
Yeah, that's it. And you were alternating around that time, huh?
Yeah. I had, as I said, the commercial band. My job was to play just anything that wasn't Dixieland, just the opposite.
Well who was there with you at the famous door?

I had George Hartman played bass and trumpet doubled, and Roger Johnson, who was deceased, played drums, and Charlie Hewitt played piano. And Jackie Blaine sang, and the boy was Billy McCree, Irish tenor. And we had to play everything that Schalke didn't play, just the opposite. That was my orders, don't play Andy Dixieland. Don't encroach on Schalke's territory.
How old was Roger Johnson when he died? He was quite young.
Oh yeah. Roger, well he was in his forties, I'd say about 46.

I remember the day that happened I was talking about him with Bob Coquille and Paul Crawford. We were over at the French market having coffee, and we were talking about how Roger was just working too hard.
He was an excellent drummer too, but he worked at it. When he played he worked, boy. He tried, you know.
Yeah. I think he was working days too, wasn't he?
No, I don't think. Not then when he knew he was going to die. He was supposed to give up smoking, give up drinking, and he said, well you've got to go and die once, and so he did.
It's funny, we were talking about him and we didn't know he'd, uh, we didn't know he'd passed. We were talking about how I guess this is he was dying. That was a fantastic job.

He had worked with me before Nick's, I mean before our famous dog. He worked with me at the Moulin Rouge, which is now Ciro's. Oh yeah. Playing shows in there for a while in the Latin Quarter where I first used George to ride, gave George his first job on Bourbon Street. He never did forget the fact. I didn't know that. George offered me a job every time, the whole time he was in the famous door, every time he'd see me he'd say, when are you going to come to work with me?
Every time he saw me.
He was a fine boy, a lot of talent. Fantastic lip.
How many could get those notes?
Well he was a fine showman, good entertainer. Was he a reader much? Not too much, no.
I think he played with some big bands.

Yeah but you learn the parts more or less, you learn the parts by memory or you know, you just, what is it called, woodshed them until you know the things and it's just a reputation, playing the same thing over, you see.
Oh, when the machine was off we were talking about some of your favorite clarinet players on records.
Oh, in the old times, Jimmy Darcy at one time and Don Murray.
Who did you hear them with?

Well, Don Murray with Big Spider-Bag I believe it was and Jimmy Darcy with Red Nichols on some of the records. I had quite a collection of records but when I went to New York and it seems like when I get back from New York they've all gone. It was one of those things, you know, the family didn't take care of them, they didn't see any value to them. The kids played with them and broke them and things like that.
Do you think any clarinet players influenced you much?

Yeah, well anybody, everybody is influenced by somebody else. Although I never did try to copy anybody's style, you subconsciously play like somebody else or like more than one individual, you hit things that you like that somebody else plays and you're going to imitate it without trying to. Rap, for instance, was a great influence on most clarinet players in his time, late Leon Rapolo. He influenced a lot, Sidney Ayrton influenced a lot of clarinet players. He played wonderfully.
A lot of things I hear him do I hear on records by other guys, I think. Oh yeah. I think the Chicago guys picked something from him.

He originated that false fingering on clarinet. And when I was at Nick's in New York, Nick used to tell me that his two favorite clarinet players were Sidney Ayrton and myself, because Sidney had worked there for quite a while. And well, Fasola he went without saying, you know, everybody liked him.
Did Nick ever play with the band much?

Oh yeah, Nick played piano, you see. And he had two pianos on the stand for that purpose, so he could come and sit in and play. And if he'd look at the keys, he'd miss, he couldn't play, he'd have to look up at the ceiling while he played. And he'd look up at the ceiling and just keep playing, boy, and he'd get a tremendous kick out of that. And Ted Husing used to come in quite a while, quite a bit every so often, maybe two, three times a week. And Billy Hill, the old songwriter that did, the one who wrote the Last Roundup and Old Spinning Wheel and those things, he was quite a fan of ours.
Now Nick, was the piano playing on the nightclub? I can't understand that. You mean the piano was in tune?
Yes, he kept two pianos on the stand. One was for him to play on. Two uprights.
Was that the only job he ever played where the piano was in tune? Yeah.
Oh yeah, well he kept them in tune purposely, you know.
That's something that's really awful here, you know.

You probably know, it's Paul Edouard Smith, or is it Edouard Smith? Charles Edouard. Charles Edouard Smith, yeah. He was quite a fan of ours and when I came back home, he came back all the way down to New Orleans to hear me play again, he told me. He liked my little register so much. He had some job for the government, wasn't it in Washington?
He was writing for the Department of Agriculture.
Yeah, something like that.
He's still going strong, still writing in New Orleans. He is? He's got things in several books out now. Of course he's an editor of that Jazzman, which I thought was a good book for its time.

Seeing Buddy Rich in town reminds me that I had a write-up in Metronome magazine, Buddy Rich and myself in the same column, saying youngsters who you must watch in the future. And they mentioned myself and Buddy Rich in the same column.
What year was that? Oh, about 38.
About 38?
We'll have to find that.
I think I have a copy of it at home. You could just get the date.
I'll make a copy of it. I'll look it up. I'll look it up and bring it to you.
I'd like to see that.

I more or less had a scrapbook, you know, of Sharky's band when we were at Nix in New York. We had a write-up by every columnist except Walter Winchell, and I don't know why. And I think we later did get one from Winchell, but I'm not sure of that.

Well to get back to the early days, you told me you played with this guy Stevens, Ernest Stevens, and you played some other little jobs. Do you remember the names of the other bands you worked with, Ernest Stevens?

There were so many. There was a little pickup band I used to play with, fellas back in Gentilly. Now that section's all paved now, but in those days it was mud streets, mud roads, and we went to a job one night on Frenchman near Gentilly Boulevard, and we got stuck in the mud there. It was a T-model Ford. I mean, you just couldn't get through. We had to walk the last way to the—and the thing was given in a barn. A dairy. A dairy barn full of cows. And we played—we played for a dance in the thing on the mud floor. People were dancing right on the mud.
Did the cows like the music?
Well, they didn't seem to mind it. I mean, they didn't do anything about it. They just stayed in their stalls while we played our jazz, you know.

One time I was following a colored parade in Marrero, you know, the jazz band. And they passed the dairy farm and the cows followed the band. They must have liked it. Must have influenced them some kind of way. And they would dance along, you know. That was funny. Fortunately, there's a movie of that. A friend of mine made a movie of that. You'd have to see the movie to believe it. I could imagine. That's pretty fantastic.

I went on the road there one year with Frank Silverhead, the head of band one time. And we played in more bonds and tobacco bonds and things all around Georgia and South Carolina and Tennessee and Florida, all the southern states, you know. We went as far as South Carolina. The band was sponsored by the Tesh Greyhound Company. And they finished the transportation and naturally we called it a band, the Tesh Greyhound Band, you know. And we played all around, all southern Louisiana, all Lafayette and Lake Charles, all that section, and then moved up. Spent the whole summer on the road, one-nighters.
Were they mostly New Orleans guys?

All New Orleans. All New Orleans colors. Al Belanco played trumpet and Earl Danton, saxophone, I played alto, lead alto and who was it? Tony Costa I believe played tenor. And Johnny Castang played drums. Frank Federico, and later we ended up with Louis Prima for quite a while. Federico and Castang, myself. Played with Louis quite a while here. Before Louis gave the band up to go to New York, then I took over the band.
Where was that at?

We had, originally there were a place called Beverly Gardens, still called Beverly Gardens, the street in Metry. And there was a club out there, Leon Prima bought the club. And Louis had the band, we played with him quite a while. Then we moved, moved in town here where they, it was a Toyssey's restaurant and they remodeled it and made a nightclub of it. Called it Prima's and then later the Shim Sham and later the Moulin Rouge on Bourbon Street. We're Syros now, has it. We worked there quite a while. You worked with Leon a while too, didn't you? Yeah, I worked with Leon at the 500 Club quite a while. I remember that.
A couple years. I was here. See, what years were those?
That's right after, I played at the St. Charles Theater for three seasons. That's right after that, that was around 48 I think. Around that time. Let's see, I think, yeah around that time.
Were you with Sharky before you went with Leon Prima? Yeah, I was with Sharky in 1936, 1937.
No, I mean in the, well you were alternating with Sharky at the Famous Door.
In between that time somewhere as you see, in around that time.

Around that time, yeah that's how I remember. Yeah, because I had played at the 500 Club with my own band and then I left the 500 Club and went to Dan's and from Dan's I went to the Famous Door and then I worked at the Latin Quarter and I think then I went back to the 500 Club with Leon then.
When did you go into Pete Herman's?

Well, the first, I worked at Pete Herman three different times. The first time when I went to New York he wanted me to put a band in his place and I told him I was all set to go to New York. But when I came back, 1940, I had a band in Pete Herman's and when the war came out I left to go to work in a shipyard. I left Pete Herman's. And I did him a very nice favor by putting all four F-men on the job and left. You know, fellas that wouldn't be called into the draft. Like Irwin Dennis who weighed almost 300 pounds, they didn't want him, you know.
Yeah, I don't know.
Yeah, and the drummer's still there incidentally. Who's that?
Charlie Stowe.

He's still working at Pete Herman's. It's 17 or 18 years now. His only job, his first union job. And when I hired him I put him in the union and he said, you think this job would be steady? I said, well I think so. I mean I couldn't guarantee him but it seems the story turned out to be steady, huh? Eighteen years. Yeah.
Who was in the band there then when you first started, Pete Herman?

Well I had five men. I had Louis Escobedo, at that time I had Bob Doyle on piano, and Charlie Stowe, and I had a bass player by the name of Lonnie Mitchell from Texas, who later was replaced by Johnny Bell. Remember Johnny Bell? You probably heard of him. He played bass. He died some years ago. But a nice little group, five pieces. Then Louis left, Louis Escobedo left, and I got Bill McElhaney. Bill's playing at WSM in Nashville. He's the staff arranger. Very fine trumpet player. Then Pete Herman closed for remodeling so I didn't go back. It took too long to come back so Fazola organized the band and I went with him. Four saxes and three or four brass, a big band, you know, and we waited for quite a while. And then Fazola saw the end in sight for the job so he tipped me off. He says, I don't think we would be on this job too much longer. The business looks pretty bad so that's all I needed was a little hint. So I accepted the job at the St. Charles Theater and incidentally played every chair in the sax section. I started on fourth tenor, moved to second tenor, and then moved to third alto and ended up playing lead alto. I worked there three years and then from there I went back to the 500 Club.
Who was in Fazola's band?

Al Hurt, Julian Lane, Al's brother, Slick Hurt, and Johnny Ronica, myself. Who else? Steve Jarrett Tanner played tenor, and Fazola, four saxes. Al Hurt and who else now? Wimpy Miller, Wimp is a lawyer you know.
Pete Lauderman.
And I kind of remember the bass and the drums.
All local boys of course.
Well Charlie Duke played with him for a while. Charlie Duke, Charlie Duke, was it? Yeah I think Charlie was playing drums with us.
The Bonnie Franks played with him for a while.
Yeah, well it might have been those two, because then they later organized, made up that Basin Street Six, you see, and they joined them.
It seems to me that's just about the same band that recorded for Victor. The Basin Street Six? No, the Fazola band recorded for Victor.
Well I didn't make recordings with him, because I think he made recordings later. I was playing at the St. Charles Stadium, and he just got more or less the same group that he had before, you see.
Well they were playing at the, see I was down here in 45 and 46, I was in the Navy, and I heard Fazola at the Plaza Club. Yeah that's the place.
Were you working with him? Yeah I worked at the Plaza with him.
And then after that he made the record, back in Georgia.

Yeah I remember now, later. The record was made later, and I couldn't make it because I was tied up in a two-year theater from one o'clock in the afternoon to eleven at night, you know, four shows a day.

Yeah, I might have heard you when I was in the Navy and didn't know you then. I remember talking to Charlie Duke out there. I think it was his wife or his girlfriend who introduced me to him. At the time I was still interested in, very interested in the band.

I played with Tony Amarica on the boat during the war too. Boy we had a heck of a band. Very good band. Lester Bouchon, Shorty Reese, Fazola and myself on saxophones. I played alto on that job too. I played lead and Fazola played third alto and Bouchon and Shorty Reese played the tenors. And Bobby Castleglough played trombone. And Red Bowman played trumpet and Howard Reed on trumpet. Alec Coulon on bass, Joe Salvaggio on piano, and Abbey Brunish, the one that died, played drums.
Sounds like a good band.
Boy was it a fine band. Really, really was it. That was a fine drummer too.
It's a shame he did one. He was playing the Sharky when he died. Supposed to fall on the Sharky's arms.
Yeah, yeah. He just played the bass. He was playing the Sharky when he died.
He was playing the Sharky's arms. He just passed out right after he ate or something like that.

He had a bad heart. Like Fazola knew he was going to die too. He quit the, what's the band now? The band had the amateur thing that Al Hurt played on. What was the band? Horace Hyde. Horace Hyde. He quit Horace Hyde to come back home, you see, so his mother could keep him on a strict diet. Well he'd eat the diet at home and come out and go to some restaurant and eat a big meal. You see, Fazola didn't die from drinking, he died from eating. He had a bad condition and he was, you know, supposed to be on a strict diet. He and I went in a restaurant in New York one day and ate and we came out walking on the street. He says, let's go in this Chinese place and get some Chinese food. I said, well, I'm full of killing him. Oh, come on. He had a big Chinese meal right on top of the other meal. He loved to eat. And I think that's what killed him, the food, you know.
That's what the hell is saying. Everybody says it.
He ate himself to death. And he was a young man, he shouldn't have died that young. For instance, look at me. Almost three years ago I was given up for death.
I bet you were pretty sick that morning.
Forty-four pints of blood.
Well, what about Coulomb? Did he die?
Yeah, Alec died recently. Well, he was kind of old, though. Alec was close to seventy.
And was Chink Martin still holding up? He was one of the oldest. He's very old.
Old Chink's very old. I think at least seventy-five now, at least.
He was playing with the-
He played with Sharky quite a while. He played with a lot of the bands. I mean he played with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. The Halfway House.
He was with Tony Almarico for a while. When I was down here during the war I heard him.
That's right.
I guess it was after the war.
Well Chink was very active for a long time. He played with all the best bands around town.
He had some talent around him in his day.
He's played through a lot of talent.
Did you ever work with Charlie Cordillo?
Yeah, not too much because he played the same instrument. I mean in those, like in smaller bands they were very seldom usable, one clarinet or sax. But Charlie played excellent clarinet.
Well that's a man that's played with good bands and has never gotten much recognition. That's funny you know.

Charlie Cordella and another one is, well let me think, he and Charlie worked together quite a while. Years ago there was a band at Pete Hermans before I ever went there. Sharky had the band I believe. Chink Martin played in it and Freddie Newman and Charlie Cordella and Sidney Ayrton played together. And then another boy, Ray, he played very well and he never did get any recognition either.
What instrument was he?
He played clarinet and sax. Ray, uh. Not Ray Burke?
No, no, no.
Harry Raymond? No, this was Italian boy. You know I know his name, I can't think of it. I'll come to you in a minute.
Yeah I probably will.
I'll come to you.
Did I ask you about any music you heard in church? No you didn't. Did your church have any training? Did you sing in church? No I never did.
My children did.
Your children did. What religion are you?

A Catholic. In fact I have a, my daughter is a nun, my oldest daughter. She sings in a choir now. And she has a very flexible voice of about three octaves, which is quite phenomenal I think. She sings soprano and turns right around and sings the alto part, either one.
That's funny. She must really have a voice to do that.
She has a very, very long extended range, three octaves.
It seems to me people are getting more training in music now. Yeah.

Through the schools and the religion, the church. We lived over in Slidell for quite a while you know, and we used to attend services at the little church there, and the priest used to always thank my little girl for being in the choir because sometimes she was the only one up there to sing you know. And both of them used to go up there and sing. In fact the younger one now is practicing with a trio, two other girls and herself, you know, and then we had to wake up some stuff. Of course on the rock and roll side, but.
Well the Bonneville sisters did well in their day here with that same type of setup. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
You mentioned Pansy Lane out there.

Yeah I played quite a bit with Pansy Lane in those days. We used to play on Esplanade Avenue, there was a place called the Eagles home. We used to play there every Saturday. And the band was up on the platform right under a tin roof. And you talk about loud, and Pansy never did play soft, you see. And none of the band played soft. Boy it used to ring so loud you couldn't hear yourself think, you know. And the only one I remember in that band was Chink Martin's brother who played bass. Bill Abraham, William Abraham, his last name is Abraham. Chief Martin's right name is Martin Abraham. And Pansy Lane carried a gun all the time. He had some special officer's badge. And every once in a while he'd pull out the gun and say, if you hit the bad note again I'm going to shoot you. Bill used to have fits, he was scared to death of that kind of thing. Boy what a ball that was. And all the old jazz tunes and Pansy used to like to play double eagle and those kind of marches in jazz time. I played with him, well off and on every spot job, you know, from time to time. But I haven't seen him in the last few years now.
Well he's passed on.
Oh he did? That's right. That's right. Boykin's transfer company I believe, then Shane for years. He just played on the side, you know.
Well they had the wig down on Elysian Fields at Shane's.
Yeah I think I remember now, now that you mention it, it comes back to me that he died.
Did you play with many loud bands in those days?
They practically were all loud. There were no microphones. I mean you had to play loud to be heard. Then we used to use a megaphone.
